title: Who are our customers?
brief: I started on Monday and nobody gave me the customer list. It is all in the company database. Can you build me a machine that pulls the names and cities?

skill.title: SELECT reads columns from a table
skill.card: A database keeps data in tables. SELECT picks the columns you want, FROM names the table.

task: Return the name and city of every row in customers.

title: Only the Lyon customers
brief: Great list. I am visiting Lyon on Thursday. I only need the customers there, with their email so I can write to them first.

skill.title: WHERE keeps only the rows you want
skill.card: WHERE comes after FROM and keeps rows whose condition is true. Text goes between single quotes.
skill.example: SELECT name, stock FROM products WHERE category = 'Furniture';

task: Return name and email of the customers whose city is Lyon.
solution: SELECT name, email FROM customers WHERE city = 'Lyon';
hint: Add WHERE city = 'Lyon' before the semicolon.

title: The five latest orders
brief: Every Monday the team asks me what came in last. I do not want the whole order book, just the five most recent orders, newest on top.

skill.title: ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT cuts
skill.card: Rows come back in no promised order. ORDER BY col sorts them, add DESC for biggest first. LIMIT n keeps the first n rows, and SELECT DISTINCT shows each value once.
skill.example: SELECT name, price FROM products ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 3;

task: Return id, customer_id, ordered and status of the 5 most recent orders, newest first (sort on ordered).
starter: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered, status FROM orders;
solution: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered, status FROM orders ORDER BY ordered DESC LIMIT 5;
hint: ORDER BY ordered DESC, then LIMIT 5.

title: First quarter orders not paid yet
brief: I am closing the first quarter. I need every order placed between January 1st and March 31st that is still pending or shipped, so not paid. My auditor arrives at ten.

skill.title: IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and IS NULL
skill.card: IN ('a', 'b') matches one value of a list, BETWEEN x AND y an inclusive range (dates stored as 'YYYY-MM-DD' work too), LIKE 'C%' a text pattern. A missing value is NULL: test it with IS NULL, never = NULL.
skill.example: SELECT name, city FROM customers WHERE city IN ('Lille', 'Nantes') AND email IS NULL;

task: Return id, customer_id, ordered and status of orders whose ordered date is between 2026-01-01 and 2026-03-31 and whose status is pending or shipped.
starter: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending';
hint: ordered BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-03-31' AND status IN ('pending', 'shipped')

title: Only what is still pending
brief: Small change on the Monday list. The team only cares about orders still pending, and they want the oldest first so nothing waits too long. Give me all of them, not just five.
task: Return id, customer_id, ordered and status of every order whose status is pending, oldest ordered date first.
solution: SELECT id, customer_id, ordered, status FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY ordered;
hint: Swap DESC LIMIT 5 for a WHERE on status and a plain ORDER BY ordered.

title: Stock level labels
brief: My pickers read raw numbers all day and miss the empty shelves. I want a word next to every product instead. Services have no stock at all, label them too.

skill.title: CASE labels rows, COALESCE fills gaps
skill.card: CASE WHEN cond THEN a WHEN cond2 THEN b ELSE c END AS name makes a computed column: the first true branch wins. COALESCE(a, b) gives the first value that is not NULL, handy for defaults.
skill.example: SELECT name, COALESCE(email, 'no email') AS contact, CASE WHEN tier = 'standard' THEN 'no' ELSE 'yes' END AS vip FROM customers;

task: Return name, stock and stock_level for every product. stock_level is 'service' when stock is NULL, 'sold out' when it is 0, 'reorder' below 10, otherwise 'ok'.
solution:
SELECT name, stock,
       CASE WHEN stock IS NULL THEN 'service'
            WHEN stock = 0 THEN 'sold out'
            WHEN stock < 10 THEN 'reorder'
            ELSE 'ok' END AS stock_level
FROM products;
hint: Test IS NULL first: CASE WHEN stock IS NULL THEN 'service' WHEN stock = 0 THEN ...

title: Payroll in one line
brief: The bank wants a payroll summary for our credit line. One line is enough: how many people, what we pay in total each month, and the average, lowest and highest salary.

skill.title: Aggregates squash rows into one value
skill.card: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) only the non NULL values. SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX work on a column, and ROUND(x, 2) keeps two decimals.
skill.example: SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(stock), ROUND(AVG(price), 2) FROM products;

task: In one row return the number of employees, the sum of salary, the average salary rounded to 2 decimals, the lowest and the highest salary, in that order.
solution: SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(salary), ROUND(AVG(salary), 2), MIN(salary), MAX(salary) FROM employees;
hint: SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(salary), ROUND(AVG(salary), 2), MIN(salary), MAX(salary) FROM employees;

title: Labels for the physical shelves only
brief: The labels work. Now the shelf printer: it only does Hardware and Furniture, and it needs the category printed too. Services can go, they never sit on a shelf.
task: Same stock_level rules, but return name, category, stock and stock_level, only for products whose category is Hardware or Furniture.
solution:
SELECT name, category, stock,
       CASE WHEN stock IS NULL THEN 'service'
            WHEN stock = 0 THEN 'sold out'
            WHEN stock < 10 THEN 'reorder'
            ELSE 'ok' END AS stock_level
FROM products
WHERE category IN ('Hardware', 'Furniture');
hint: Add category to the SELECT and WHERE category IN ('Hardware', 'Furniture') after FROM.

title: What do customers call about?
brief: I am rewriting our help pages and want to start with what hurts most. Count the tickets per subject, and only show the subjects with 4 tickets or more, the biggest first.

skill.title: GROUP BY counts per group, HAVING filters groups
skill.card: GROUP BY col runs the aggregate once per value of col. WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters the groups after.
skill.example: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders WHERE status <> 'cancelled' GROUP BY status HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

task: Return subject and n (number of tickets) for each subject that has at least 4 tickets, highest n first, then by subject.
starter: SELECT subject, COUNT(*) AS n FROM tickets;
solution:
SELECT subject, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM tickets
GROUP BY subject
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4
ORDER BY n DESC, subject;
hint: GROUP BY subject HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4 ORDER BY n DESC, subject

title: Payroll per department
brief: The bank liked the summary, and now the board wants it per department. Same idea, one line per department. People without a department show up on their own line, that is fine.
task: Return dept_id, headcount (number of employees) and payroll (sum of salary) for each dept_id, ordered by dept_id.
solution:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS headcount, SUM(salary) AS payroll
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;
hint: GROUP BY dept_id, and ORDER BY dept_id.

title: Pending orders with real names
brief: The pending list is useful but the team cannot read customer ids. Put the customer name next to each pending order so they can pick up the phone.

skill.title: JOIN stitches tables back together
skill.card: Tables point at each other with ids. JOIN other ON other.id = t.other_id glues each row to its match. Short aliases (orders o) keep it readable. An inner join drops rows with no match.
skill.example: SELECT o.id, c.name, o.status FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id LIMIT 3;

task: Return the order id, the customer name and the ordered date of every order whose status is pending.
solution:
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.ordered
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'pending';
hint: JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id, then select c.name.

title: Customers who never ordered
brief: Some customers signed up and then went quiet. I want to call them this week with an offer. Who has never placed a single order?

skill.title: LEFT JOIN keeps the rows without a match
skill.card: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table. When nothing matches, the right side columns are NULL, so WHERE right.id IS NULL finds what has no partner.
skill.example: SELECT p.name, oi.id FROM products p LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id LIMIT 5;

task: Return the name, city and email of customers who have no order at all.
solution:
SELECT c.name, c.city, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
hint: LEFT JOIN orders, then keep WHERE o.id IS NULL.

title: Top five customers
brief: The CEO asked me who our best customers are and I said "the usual ones". Not good enough. Give me the five biggest by revenue, cancelled orders do not count.

skill.title: Joins chain across many tables
skill.card: To go from a customer to what they bought, walk the links: customers, orders, order_items. Each JOIN adds one hop, then GROUP BY turns the lines into totals.
skill.example: SELECT c.name, oi.qty, oi.unit_price FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id LIMIT 4;

task: Return each customer name and revenue (sum of qty * unit_price from order_items, rounded to 2 decimals) for orders whose status is not cancelled. Highest revenue first, 5 rows.
solution:
SELECT c.name, ROUND(SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY c.id
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 5;
hint: customers, orders, order_items: two JOINs, then GROUP BY c.id ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 5.

title: Orders with no payment
brief: Cash is tight this month. Find me every order that is not cancelled but has no payment recorded, with the customer name, so I can send reminders.
task: Return the order id, the customer name, the ordered date and the status of orders that are not cancelled and have no row in payments, oldest first.
starter:
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.ordered, o.status
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
ORDER BY o.ordered;
solution:
SELECT o.id, c.name, o.ordered, o.status
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled' AND p.id IS NULL
ORDER BY o.ordered;
hint: Add LEFT JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id and keep p.id IS NULL.

title: Revenue per tier instead
brief: Change of plan from the CEO: she does not want names, she wants to know if our gold and platinum tiers are worth the discounts. Same revenue, but one line per tier, and all tiers.
task: Return tier, customers (number of distinct customers who ordered) and revenue (rounded to 2 decimals, non cancelled orders) per customer tier, highest revenue first.
solution:
SELECT c.tier, COUNT(DISTINCT c.id) AS customers, ROUND(SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY c.tier
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
hint: GROUP BY c.tier instead of c.id, drop the LIMIT, and count customers with COUNT(DISTINCT c.id).
